section_summary: This section consists chiefly of letters, petitions, resolutions, and telegrams from American religious leaders, educators, students, civic groups, and private citizens demanding restrictions or an embargo on exports of arms, aircraft, oil, scrap iron, and other war materials to Japan. State Department replies repeatedly explain that, without a presidential finding that a state of war existed between China and Japan, the Neutrality Act supplied no authority to prohibit arms exports, while non-munitions commodities lay outside the Act altogether. The papers also document missionary reports of Japanese bombing, export-license statistics, a discussion with missionary John C. Hawk, and several related acknowledgments and cross-reference sheets.

subfiles.title: Kuomintang inquiry concerning American war supplies shipped to Japan
subfiles.from: Wilbur W. H. Pyn, Kuomintang of China in America, New York Branch
subfiles.about: Pyn asks for the amounts and types of war supplies shipped from the United States to Japan since July 1937.
subfiles.summary: New York Kuomintang committee renews its request for an embargo on aircraft and war materials for Japan, thanking Hull for protesting destruction of American property in China.

subfiles.title: Reply to Wilbur W. H. Pyn
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department directs Pyn to seek the requested export information from the Chinese Embassy.
subfiles.summary: Yost acknowledges Pyn's July 21 inquiry and suggests the Chinese Embassy in Washington for export statistics.

subfiles.title: Percy A. Darling’s appeal to President Roosevelt
subfiles.from: Percy A. Darling
subfiles.about: Darling asks what the administration is doing to prevent arms and war materials from reaching aggressor nations, especially Japan.
subfiles.summary: Darling, a past Roosevelt supporter, asks how the government is stopping American materials being used in Japan's bombing of China.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Percy A. Darling
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: Yost explains the legal limits of the Neutrality Act and the administration’s decision not to proclaim a state of war between China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Reply to Darling: a proclamation would bar arms to both China and Japan, no authority without one; Roosevelt judged invocation against broader interests; license values and Hull's condemnation of civilian bombing.

subfiles.title: David Burcham’s protest against strategic exports to Japan
subfiles.from: David Burcham, Polytechnic High School
subfiles.about: Burcham asks how Americans can stop exports of oil, scrap iron, cotton, and armaments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Burcham deplores destruction in China, says ending strategic shipments could stop the war within three months, and asks what citizens can do.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to David Burcham
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains why neither the Neutrality Act nor existing presidential authority could stop all of the exports Burcham named.
subfiles.summary: Yost: a war proclamation would embargo arms to both sides, non-arms commodities are outside it; licensed exports about $13.97 million to China and $10.38 million to Japan.

subfiles.title: Conversation with missionary John C. Hawk
subfiles.from: Joseph W. Ballantine, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Hawk discusses his planned speaking campaign against munitions shipments to Japan and requests statistics and policy advice.
subfiles.summary: Missionary John Hawk asks if 54 percent of Japan's imported war supplies come from the US; Ballantine declines to confirm or advise on repealing the Neutrality Act but offers commodity statistics.

subfiles.title: Morristown District resolutions and request for an audience with John C. Hawk
subfiles.from: E. A. Shugart, Morristown District, Methodist Episcopal Church, South
subfiles.about: Shugart transmits resolutions seeking an end to the war in China and a meeting between Hull and missionary John C. Hawk.
subfiles.summary: Morristown District clergy ask Hull to hear John Hawk on the undeclared war, citing his thirty-two years in China.

subfiles.title: Appointment for John C. Hawk
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.about: The Department confirms an appointment for John C. Hawk on July 21.
subfiles.summary: Dr. Hawk is given an appointment at eleven o'clock on July 21, replying to Shugart's July 12 letter.

subfiles.title: C. C. Gilbert’s request that Hull receive John C. Hawk
subfiles.from: C. C. Gilbert
subfiles.about: Gilbert asks Hull to meet briefly with missionary John C. Hawk during the following week.
subfiles.summary: Gilbert asks Hull to receive missionary John Hawk, home on furlough after thirty years in China, and to wire the Battery Park Hotel.

subfiles.title: Hull’s telegram agreeing to see John C. Hawk
subfiles.from: Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Hull agrees to receive Hawk on Thursday, July 21, at eleven o’clock.
subfiles.summary: The official telegram responds affirmatively to Gilbert’s request. It fixes the meeting for July 21 at 11:00 a.m.

subfiles.title: John C. Hawk’s travel confirmation
subfiles.from: John C. Hawk
subfiles.about: Hawk reports that he plans to arrive in Washington for the scheduled conference.
subfiles.summary: The short telegram confirms Hawk’s intended arrival in Washington on Thursday morning. He thanks Hull for arranging the conference.

subfiles.title: Garbled attaché report concerning radio communications
subfiles.from: Unidentified attaché or reporting officer
subfiles.about: The heavily corrupted report appears to concern radio communications, a Cairo radio conference, coded abbreviations, and possibly unauthorized dispatches.
subfiles.summary: Garbled attaché report apparently on control of radio stations or circuits and a radio conference; OCR too damaged to be sure.

subfiles.title: American Red Cross acknowledgment of State Department enclosures
subfiles.from: Secretary, American Red Cross
subfiles.about: The Red Cross acknowledges receipt of a joint resolution and the pamphlet International Traffic in Arms.
subfiles.summary: American Red Cross acknowledges Hull's July 21 letter and two enclosures, forwarded to Norman Davis.

subfiles.title: Egbert W. Smith’s appeal to halt war supplies to Japan
subfiles.from: Egbert W. Smith, Presbyterian Church in the United States
subfiles.about: Smith urges action to end American material support for Japan and quotes a missionary’s description of the bombing of Haichow.
subfiles.summary: Smith praises Hull’s trade-agreement program but reports widespread indignation over American supplies used in Japan’s campaign in China. Quoting a Haichow missionary, he describes almost continuous air raids that killed civilians while missing soldiers and argues that relief work is inconsistent with continuing to equip the aggressor.

subfiles.title: Hull’s reply to Egbert W. Smith
subfiles.from: Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Hull explains the Neutrality Act, export-license figures, and his public opposition to aerial bombing of civilians.
subfiles.summary: Hull thanks Smith for backing reciprocal trade agreements; a war proclamation would embargo arms to both sides, ordinary commodities uncovered; licenses about $13.97 million to China, $10.38 million to Japan.

subfiles.title: New Salem correspondent’s criticism of the administration’s export policy
subfiles.from: Unidentified correspondent in New Salem, Massachusetts
subfiles.about: An unidentified writer attacks the legal and moral reasoning used to permit continued war-supply exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: New Salem writer says refusing to recognize a state of war aligns the US with Japan, welcomes declining licenses as partly a boycott effect, and wants immediate export controls even with compensation.

subfiles.title: George C. Warren on arms distribution to China and Japan
subfiles.from: George C. Warren
subfiles.about: Warren thanks Yost for the Neutrality Act material and expresses hope that shipments to countries at war in fact could be suspended.
subfiles.summary: Warren is pleased distribution to China exceeded that to Japan but wishes exports could stop without a formal declaration of war.

subfiles.title: Bishop Ralph S. Cushman’s telegram urging an end to exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Ralph S. Cushman
subfiles.about: Cushman urges Roosevelt and the State Department to use every legal measure to stop iron, oil, military vehicles, and other war materials from reaching Japan.
subfiles.summary: Bishop Ralph Cushman telegraphs that public opinion would support strong restrictions on exports of iron, oil and war automobiles to Japan.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Bishop Ralph S. Cushman
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost outlines the legal limits on restricting arms and commodity exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The reply explains that invocation of the Neutrality Act would prohibit arms sales to China as well as Japan and that no authority existed to embargo other commodities. It says Roosevelt had decided invocation was not in the country’s overall interest and provides the standard export-license totals for both belligerents.

subfiles.title: Georgianna Richards’s acknowledgment for Miss Woolley
subfiles.from: Georgianna Richards
subfiles.about: Richards acknowledges materials sent to Miss Woolley while Woolley is attending a meeting in London.
subfiles.summary: Georgianna Richards says Miss Woolley is in London at the International Federation of University Women and will reply after returning in late August.

subfiles.title: Helen Bell’s protest against exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Helen Bell
subfiles.about: Bell protests American shipments of oil, scrap iron, and airplanes that sustain Japan’s war in China.
subfiles.summary: Helen Bell, eighteen and unable to vote, protests exports essential to Japan's campaign and says State should pressure exporters.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Helen Bell
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: The Department explains why existing law did not permit the requested embargo and cites its opposition to bombing civilians.
subfiles.summary: Yost states that without a presidential proclamation no legal basis existed to stop arms exports to Japan and that the Neutrality Act did not cover ordinary commodities. He gives export-license totals for China and Japan and recalls Hull’s June 11 statement condemning civilian bombing and those who materially encouraged it.

subfiles.title: Second Reformed Church letter and petition for an embargo on Japan
subfiles.from: William Louis Sahler and petitioners in Freehold, New Jersey
subfiles.about: Sahler transmits signatures supporting an embargo on airplanes and all materials usable in Japanese war production.
subfiles.summary: The petition argues that supplying airplanes and munitions materials makes Americans partners in the killing of Chinese men, women, and children. It asks Hull to embargo everything sent to Japan that might be used in producing war supplies and includes several pages of signatures.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to William Louis Sahler and petitioners
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: Yost acknowledges the Freehold petition and explains the limits of the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: The Department promises careful consideration but says an arms embargo required a presidential finding of war and would bind both China and Japan. It also states that the Act could not prohibit non-arms commodities and reiterates Hull’s condemnation of civilian bombing and its material encouragement.

subfiles.title: William F. Quillian’s appeal for an embargo on Japan
subfiles.from: William F. Quillian, General Board of Christian Education
subfiles.about: Quillian reports growing concern among church leaders and advocates an embargo on war supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Quillian condemns Japan's campaign as ruthless, trusts Hull, and finds policy toward China hard to reconcile with that toward Spain.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to William F. Quillian
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Moore explains the administration’s decision not to invoke the Neutrality Act against China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: The response states that declaring a state of war would immediately stop arms exports to both countries, while the absence of a proclamation left no legal authority for an embargo on Japan alone. It emphasizes presidential discretion and broader national interests and supplies comparative export-license figures.

subfiles.title: Texas Federation of Women’s Clubs protest against war-material sales
subfiles.from: Mrs. Richard J. Turrentine
subfiles.about: Turrentine urges immediate action against sales of war materials to Japan, particularly supplies used in bombing cities.
subfiles.summary: Texas Federation of Women's Clubs president, after a devastating bombing apparently at Canton, fears American munitions are being used but praises Hull for preserving peace.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Mrs. Richard J. Turrentine
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost sets out the Neutrality Act explanation and comparative export-license totals.
subfiles.summary: The reply says an arms embargo depended on a presidential war proclamation and would apply equally to China and Japan. It adds that Roosevelt had concluded invocation was not in the broader interests of the United States and gives the Department’s standard license figures.

subfiles.title: Calvary Methodist Episcopal Church statement on China and American foreign policy
subfiles.from: Official Board, Calvary Methodist Episcopal Church, Wichita
subfiles.about: The church calls for invocation of neutrality legislation, tighter controls on supplies and credit, condemnation of civilian bombing, and delay of naval expansion.
subfiles.summary: The statement says relief fundraising cannot address suffering while American materials enable Japan’s attacks on China. It urges an embargo on the aggressor, supervision of credits, an international economic conference, vigorous protest against bombing noncombatants, and diversion of some armament spending toward arbitration and peaceful settlement.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to the Calvary Methodist Episcopal Church
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: Yost acknowledges the church board’s views and defends the decision not to invoke the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: The response promises careful consideration of the board’s positions on China, foreign policy, and naval policy. It says Roosevelt judged invocation contrary to American interests, gives export-license totals, and points to Hull’s public condemnation of civilian bombing and the manufacturers supplying bombing planes.

subfiles.title: W. P. Ladd on Spain and Japan
subfiles.from: W. P. Ladd, Berkeley Divinity School
subfiles.about: Ladd protests the lack of ordinary trade with the Spanish government and the continued flow of assistance to Japan against China.
subfiles.summary: W. P. Ladd, a lifelong Republican, criticizes administration policy on Spain and Japan, saying views are widely shared in New Haven.

subfiles.title: Hull’s reply to W. P. Ladd
subfiles.from: Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Hull gives a detailed legal explanation of the Spanish arms embargo and the absence of a comparable embargo on Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hull explains that Spain alone was then subject to an arms embargo, imposed by the January 8, 1937 joint resolution and removable only by Congress or by a finding that the civil conflict had ended. For China and Japan, he states that no presidential finding of war had been made, non-arms commodities could not be prohibited, and broader national interests counseled against invoking the Act. The file includes alternate final-page language with both older and updated export-license figures.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to memorandum on commercial credits for arms sales to Japan
subfiles.from: Department of State, J. Green
subfiles.about: The sheet directs researchers to a memorandum about National City Bank credits intended to facilitate arms sales to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: memorandum on talks with Rentschler and Lancaster of National City Bank; no credits for arms sales to Japan would survive a Neutrality Act proclamation.

subfiles.title: York Springs Church of God appeal for peace and reduced armaments
subfiles.from: Walter Miller, York Springs Church of God
subfiles.about: The church protests belligerent policies, naval expansion, and conduct that might draw the United States into another world war.
subfiles.summary: York Springs Church of God urges stopping supplies to the East Asian conflict, opposes Pacific fleet expansion, and proposes sending doctors and Christian workers and redirecting battleship funds.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Walter Miller
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost explains the law governing exports to China and Japan and refers Miller to Roosevelt’s message supporting increased armaments.
subfiles.summary: Reply to Walter Miller: a war finding would embargo arms to both sides; ordinary exports beyond tin-plate scrap and helium are generally unprohibitable; encloses Roosevelt's January 1938 message.

subfiles.title: Silver Lake Epworth League Institute embargo petition
subfiles.from: Faculty and students, Silver Lake Epworth League Institute
subfiles.about: Faculty and students petition for an embargo on war materials sent to the Orient.
subfiles.summary: The surviving pages identify the Methodist Episcopal Church institute and contain an extensive list of faculty and student signatures. The Department’s subsequent reply records their request as an embargo on all war materials destined for the Orient.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to the Silver Lake petition
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Robert Horton and other Silver Lake petitioners
subfiles.about: Yost acknowledges the petition and explains why the government had not embargoed war materials to East Asia.
subfiles.summary: The response promises careful consideration but states that a presidential war proclamation would halt arms exports to both China and Japan. It explains that non-arms commodities were outside the Neutrality Act and that Roosevelt judged invocation inconsistent with the broader interests of the United States.

subfiles.title: John Warren Day’s protest against bombing and munitions trade
subfiles.from: John Warren Day, Grace Cathedral
subfiles.about: Day condemns civilian bombing in Spain and China and asks Hull to end trade that supports Japanese attacks on Canton and other cities.
subfiles.summary: John Day protests bombing of women and children, supports Hull's protests, and says American munitions make the US a partner in killing at Canton.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to John Warren Day
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost thanks Day for supporting the Department’s aviation policy and gives the standard legal explanation concerning exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Reply to Day cites policy on aeronautical equipment for countries bombing civilians; the act needs a presidential finding and would bar China too; commodities outside the arms list cannot be banned; license totals.

subfiles.title: Early Bible Class protest against munitions exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Myrtle A. Dick for the Early Bible Class
subfiles.about: The Bible class asks Roosevelt to use his authority to prohibit munitions shipments to aggressor nations such as Japan.
subfiles.summary: The writers reject the lack of a Japanese declaration of war as a pretext for profitable munitions exports. They appeal for foreign and domestic policy founded on Christian principles and urge Roosevelt to provide courageous moral leadership.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Myrtle A. Dick and the Early Bible Class
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges the class’s views and explains why Roosevelt had not invoked the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: Yost to Myrtle Dick's Bible class: a war finding would embargo both China and Japan, no Japan-only authority; invocation judged against US interests; standard license totals.

subfiles.title: Senior Bishop’s protest against war-sustaining trade with Japan
subfiles.from: Edwin Holt Hughes, Senior Bishop, Methodist Episcopal Church
subfiles.about: Hughes reports growing nationwide opposition to commerce that assists Japan’s destruction of China.
subfiles.summary: A senior bishop says war-sustaining trade with Japan is neither ethical nor consistent with friendship for China, speaking for a vast majority of Americans.
